title: Cobalt hydroxide has a $5/lb gap between bid and offer
gist: Cobalt hydroxide has stopped clearing rather than repriced: no confirmed trades in 10 days, a $17-22/lb bid stuck 23% below the $22-23/lb sell-side anchor, and Benchmark argues this frozen-not-falling state is itself a meaningful signal that wider, transaction-inclusive assessments would mask.

insights.claim: Benchmark recorded zero confirmed cobalt hydroxide trades over a 10-day period, holding its daily CIF Asia price assessment flat at $22.00-$23.00/lb even as the market visibly deteriorated underneath.
insights.speaker: Benchmark Team
insights.so_what: A flat headline price here is not stability -- it signals a market that has stopped clearing, which can precede a sharp repricing once a trade finally sets a new evidenced level.
insights.quote: Benchmark has observed no cobalt hydroxide trades over the past 10 days, leading to the daily price assessments to hold steady at $22.00–$23.00/lb.

insights.claim: Benchmark's weekly cobalt hydroxide bid-offer spread has widened to $17.00-$22.00/lb, with the bid roughly $5/lb (about 23%) below the last evidenced trade level, and no transaction has occurred anywhere in that gap.
insights.speaker: Benchmark Team
insights.so_what: An unvalidated, untested $5/lb gap is a live risk marker for anyone pricing Q4 DRC-origin offtake -- the true clearing price could land anywhere in that band.
insights.quote: the sell-side remains anchored to the level where material last actually changed hands while the buy-side has marked itself down five dollars, or roughly 23% below it
insights.locator: paragraph beginning "Put those two series side-by-side"

insights.claim: Sellers have told Benchmark they will not transact below $20.00/lb and generally need above $22.00/lb to conclude a sale, a floor consistent with the last evidenced trades and still $5/lb clear of the current bid.
insights.speaker: Benchmark Team
insights.so_what: Sell-side price floors this firm suggest sellers are not yet under enough liquidity pressure to capitulate, implying the standoff could persist rather than resolve quickly.
insights.quote: Sellers have told Benchmark that they will not transact below $20.00/lb and that they generally need something above $22.00/lb to conclude a sale

insights.claim: George Ingall, Benchmark's senior cobalt price analyst, frames the standoff as rational on both sides: DRC hydroxide sitting in Asian warehouses has carrying cost but no deadline for sellers, while buyers holding adequate inventory against a weak downstream order book have no incentive to chase price up.
insights.speaker: George Ingall
insights.so_what: Because neither side faces a forcing mechanism, the market can stay frozen (not clearing) for an extended period rather than mean-reverting quickly -- investors should not assume a fast resolution.
insights.quote: Both sides are behaving rationally, since DRC material sitting in Asian warehouses carries a cost but does not carry a deadline, and buyers holding adequate inventory against a weak downstream order book have no reason to chase

insights.claim: Ingall's core distinction is that this is a market that has stopped clearing, not one that has repriced -- repricing may still come but has not happened yet.
insights.speaker: George Ingall
insights.so_what: Watch for the first confirmed trade inside or below the current bid-offer band as the trigger event that would convert a paralysed market into a repriced one.
insights.quote: What that produces is a market which has stopped clearing rather than one which has repriced, and while the repricing may still come it has not come yet, which is the distinction that matters.

insights.claim: Benchmark's daily CIF Asia cobalt hydroxide assessment counts only confirmed, evidenced transactions -- excluding indications, sentiment, or stated willingness to deal -- so when trading stops, the series itself goes silent rather than drifting.
insights.speaker: Benchmark Team
insights.so_what: Understanding an index's construction (trade-based vs. indication-based) is essential before trusting a 'flat' or 'stable' print as a signal of actual market health.
insights.quote: Benchmark's daily CIF Asia cobalt hydroxide assessment only accounts for confirmed transactions rather than indications, sentiment, or levels at which somebody says they would be willing to deal

insights.claim: Across Q3, Benchmark's daily cobalt hydroxide assessment changed on only 6 of 40 publication days, versus 27 of 64 days in the same quarter a year earlier, showing that trade-driven repricing had been thinning for months before it stopped entirely in the most recent week.
insights.speaker: Benchmark Team
insights.so_what: A multi-month decline in trading frequency (Q3 this year vs last year) is an early warning indicator of liquidity drying up in cobalt hydroxide, worth tracking as a leading signal ahead of the current freeze.
insights.quote: Across Q3 the daily assessment has changed on just six of forty publication days, against twenty-seven of sixty-four in the same quarter last year
insights.locator: section "Why a flat trade-based price assessment is information"

insights.claim: Daniel Fletcher-Manuel, Benchmark's director of indexing and derivatives, argues that price reporting agencies which widen their range by including small, marginal intra-Chinese sales between related or affiliated parties produce a lively-looking but misleading spread, since much of that volume is effectively transfer pricing rather than genuine spot dealing.
insights.speaker: Daniel Fletcher-Manuel
insights.so_what: Traders relying on competing price benchmarks that blend affiliated-party transactions risk anchoring Q4 offtake negotiations to a spread that doesn't reflect where third-party units can actually be bought -- methodology choice materially changes the tradable signal.
insights.quote: An assessment that widens its range by sweeping in small, marginal, intra-Chinese sales between related or affiliated parties will keep printing a lively-looking spread through the same week, even though those sales are not spot in any commercially meaningful sense

insights.claim: Fletcher-Manuel's broader claim is that a wider bid-offer spread from a methodology that includes marginal/affiliated sales is often less informative than a narrower, purely trade-based range, inverting the usual assumption that more data points mean more clarity.
insights.speaker: Daniel Fletcher-Manuel
insights.so_what: Investors comparing price reporting agencies should weight assessment methodology, not just spread width, when deciding which benchmark to reference for offtake or hedging contracts.
insights.quote: A range built on that material tells a buyer with a Q4 offtake to settle almost nothing about where third-party units could actually be bought, which is why a wider spread is often not more information but less.

insights.claim: Using the European cobalt metal low of $25.00/lb as the payable reference, the last evidenced hydroxide trades imply payables of about 88-92%, while the current depressed bid implies only about 68% -- a roughly 20-point payable gap on the same specification with no transaction in between.
insights.speaker: Benchmark Team
insights.so_what: A 20-payable-point unresolved band is a direct input into DRC miners' and traders' realized revenue per tonne of hydroxide -- material enough to swing project economics depending on which end of the range eventually clears.
insights.quote: the last evidenced hydroxide trades imply payables of around 88 to 92% while the current bid implies about 68%, leaving twenty payable points on the same specification unresolved
insights.locator: paragraph beginning "Taking the European metal low"

insights.claim: Chinese cobalt sulphate prices fell 6.7% week-on-week to RMB 68,000-72,000/tonne ($10,132-$10,728/tonne), with the low end driven by recyclers offering discounted units, showing that unlike hydroxide, sulphate is actually finding a clearing price through active trading.
insights.speaker: Benchmark Team
insights.so_what: Sulphate's continued price discovery versus hydroxide's freeze is a divergence worth monitoring -- it suggests the weakness is genuinely being priced in the battery-material chain even where the raw hydroxide market has seized up.
insights.quote: Sulphate is moving, and it is instructive that it is, with prices falling 6.7% w-o-w to RMB 68,000–72,000/tonne ($10,132–$10,728/tonne)
insights.locator: section "China is discovering price, just not in hydroxide"

insights.claim: Several market participants suggested to Benchmark that domestic Chinese battery supply chain buyers are deliberately posting offers below market levels to drag the sulphate assessment down ahead of pre-Golden Week stockpiling.
insights.speaker: Benchmark Team
insights.so_what: If confirmed, this is a seasonal, tactical price-suppression pattern around China's Golden Week that traders could anticipate and fade in subsequent sulphate assessments.
insights.quote: several participants have suggested to us that domestic battery supply chain buyers are deliberately posting offers below the market in order to drag the assessment down ahead of pre-Golden Week stockpiling
insights.locator: section "China is discovering price, just not in hydroxide"

insights.claim: Cobalt metal shows a third pricing fracture: European standard grade eased 0.6% week-on-week to $25.00-$27.20/lb while Chinese domestic metal trades far lower at around $20.00-$21.00/lb, a regional gap some participants are using to rationalize the steep hydroxide bid markdown.
insights.speaker: Benchmark Team
insights.so_what: The China-vs-Europe cobalt metal price gap is being cited as justification for lower hydroxide bids, so any narrowing or widening of that regional spread could directly move sentiment in the stalled hydroxide market.
insights.quote: European standard grade easing 0.6% w-o-w to $25.00–$27.20/lb, while Chinese domestic metal is assessed at around $20.00–$21.00/lb
